MLS listing photo preflight

Check a folder of listing photos before you deliver them: resolution, file size, format, crop shape, branding in the filename, and staged-photo pairing. Your photos are read in this browser and never uploaded. Free, no signup.

Had a set kicked back? Why was my listing photo rejected? walks through the reasons that are readable from the file, and what to change.

Comparing this to a paid editing/staging service? See this checker vs. BoxBrownie.

Choose the delivery folder

Drop JPEG or PNG files here

or

Nothing leaves your device. Only each file's header is read — the image itself is never decoded or transmitted.

Findings

    One row per finding. Files with no findings are listed as passing the checks below — not as accepted by any MLS.
    FileRuleSeverityDetail

    What to fix

    Grouped by the most expensive thing each file needs. Photos with no findings are left out.

    Take the record with you

    Each export states what was and was not checked, so the limitation travels with the file.

    Skipped files

    None.

    What this checks

    RuleFloorSeverity
    Long edgeAt least 1024pxblocking
    File sizeAt most 20 MiBblocking
    FormatJPEG or PNGblocking
    Branding filenameNo logo, watermark, branded, brokerage, headshotblocking
    Staged pairingA staged file has a sibling originalblocking
    Aspect ratio4:3, 3:2, 16:9, 5:4 or 1:1 (±4%)degrading

    What this does not check

    Three things this tool deliberately cannot decide, because none of them is visible in a file header or a filename:

    • Visual watermarks. A logo drawn into the image is invisible to a header check. A file can pass the branding-filename rule and still carry branding in the picture.
    • Burned-in contact details. Same reason — a phone number rendered into the photo is pixels, not metadata.
    • Board-specific rules. Individual MLS boards set their own minimums, maximums, counts, ordering, and disclosure wording. This tool knows none of them.

    So a clean result means the mechanical floor is met and nothing more. It is not an acceptance decision, and it does not replace reading your board's current photo standards.

    Questions

    Why do MLS portals reject listing photos?

    The most common reasons are mechanical rather than artistic: the image is below the portal's minimum resolution, the file is larger than the upload cap, it is in a format the portal does not accept, it is cropped to a shape the gallery cannot use, or the filename or image carries brokerage branding, a logo, or an agent headshot. Many boards also require that a virtually staged photo be delivered alongside its unstaged original. Every one of those except the visual checks can be decided from the file itself before you upload anything.

    What resolution do listing photos need to be?

    This tool checks against a documented floor of 1024px on the long edge, which is the common minimum across mainstream portals. Individual MLS boards frequently require more, and some set a maximum as well. Treat a pass here as clearing the floor, not as meeting your specific board's rule — check your board's current photo standards for the number that actually binds you.

    Are my listing photos uploaded anywhere?

    No. The check runs entirely in your browser and reads only the first few hundred bytes of each file — the header that carries format and dimensions. The image pixels are never decoded, the files are never transmitted, and there is no server, account, or upload step. You can disconnect from the network and the tool still works.

    Does a clean preflight mean the MLS will accept my photos?

    No, and the record says so on every copy. This checks file headers and filenames only. It cannot see a watermark or burned-in contact details drawn into the image itself, and it does not know any individual board's rules. A clean result means the mechanical floor is met; a human still has to review the photos against the destination board's current standards.

    What is the staged-photo pairing check?

    Many boards require a virtually staged photo to be disclosed and delivered next to the unstaged original of the same room. This tool looks for filenames containing staged, virtually-staged, or virtual-staged, and flags any that have no sibling file with the same stem once that token is removed — for example living-staged.jpg with no living.jpg or living-original.jpg beside it. It is a filename convention check, not a detection of staging in the image.

    Disclaimer

    No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, compliance, or professional advice, and it does not replace your MLS board's current photo standards or a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

    Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice.

    Privacy

    Everything runs in your browser. Your photos are never uploaded, and we don't have accounts, tracking cookies, or an analytics vendor. This page counts anonymous, local feature-use events (e.g. "a check was completed") in your own browser's localStorage — never filenames, image data, or anything identifying — only to help this project's maintainers tell whether the tool is used at all. Nothing is sent anywhere.

    Also preflighting files before a paid delivery in a different market? The print-file preflight compares up to five print exports at a chosen size and produces a dated technical record before ordering a proof — nothing uploaded.

    Pricing the inspection on the same listing instead of the photos? The home inspection fee calculator prices a residential inspection from square footage, stories, foundation type, and home age, plus radon, sewer scope, termite/WDO, and mold add-ons — nothing uploaded there either.

MLS Listing Photo Preflight vs. BoxBrownie

Different jobs: BoxBrownie is a paid service that edits, stages, and enhances listing photos. This is a free, offline check for whether a delivery folder will get mechanically rejected before any of that editing happens.

What each one is for

BoxBrownie is a well-known online real estate photo editing service, described on its own site as offering photo enhancement, virtual staging, floor plans, and related property-marketing image services: a photographer or agent uploads source images, an editor works on them, and finished images come back, ordered and paid for per photo or per package. It is the kind of service a listing team reaches for when the photos are correctly captured but need retouching, sky replacement, decluttering, or virtual furniture added before they go live. BoxBrownie's own current pricing and turnaround times are not restated here, since this page cannot confirm today's numbers — only its well-documented category and service shape are described.

This checker does none of that. It has no editor, no upload step, and no per-photo charge. It reads each file's header and filename — never the decoded image — to answer a narrower, earlier question: will this delivery folder clear the mechanical floor a listing system actually enforces? Resolution, byte size, format, crop shape, a brokerage-branded filename, and a staged photo missing its unaltered original are all things it flags before you pay anyone to touch the images or upload them anywhere.

What each one answers.
QuestionWhere to answer it
Will this folder get bounced for being too small, too large, the wrong format, an odd crop, a branded filename, or an unpaired staged shot? This checker — free, runs in your browser, nothing uploaded, done before you send anything anywhere.
My photos are correctly shaped but the sky is blown out, the room is cluttered, or I want virtual staging or a floor plan drawn up. BoxBrownie or a comparable paid editing service — that is real editing work this checker never attempts.
Which files, specifically, need a re-export or a rename before I deliver or upload anywhere? This checker — a per-file findings table plus a downloadable evidence record naming exactly what to fix.
Do I need an account, a per-photo charge, or to send images to a third party to find out? BoxBrownie: yes, that is the service. This checker: no — nothing is uploaded and nothing is billed.

The two are complementary rather than competing: running this checker first means the folder you eventually send to BoxBrownie (or shoot yourself) is already free of the mechanical problems — wrong format, an oversized file, a stray branded filename — that would otherwise cost a re-edit or a rejected upload after the paid work is already done. This page makes no live comparison against BoxBrownie and sends it no traffic or data; it is a static page describing a publicly documented service category.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the checks run in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Questions

Should I use this checker or a service like BoxBrownie?

Most agents end up using both, for different reasons. BoxBrownie is a paid online service, described on its own site, that edits real estate photos, builds virtual staging and floor plans, and returns finished images through a human-in-the-loop editing pipeline you upload to and pay per photo. It makes a set of photos look better. This checker does not touch how a photo looks: it reads each file's header and filename in your browser to catch the mechanical reasons a delivery gets kicked back — too small, too large, wrong format, an odd crop, a branded filename, or a staged photo with no paired original — before you pay anyone to edit it or upload it anywhere. Running this first means you send a clean, correctly-shaped folder to an editing service, and you catch a branding or pairing problem for free instead of paying for a re-edit.

Is this page affiliated with BoxBrownie?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by BoxBrownie. BoxBrownie is named here only to describe what this checker is and is not.

why-was-my-listing-photo-rejected.html.text:
← MLS listing photo preflight — free checker

Why was my listing photo rejected?

A photo bounced back the afternoon a listing was supposed to go live is an expensive kind of small problem: the shoot is over, the seller is waiting, and the message usually says what failed without saying which file. Most of the reasons are mechanical — readable from the file before anyone looks at the picture — which means they are also catchable before you deliver.

Check a delivery folder — free, nothing is uploaded

The reasons you can check from the file

What bouncedWhat it usually isThe fix
Too smallA phone export, a screenshot, or an image pulled from a website rather than the delivery folderRe-export from the original. This tool's floor is 1024 px on the long edge; your board may ask for more
Wrong formatHEIC straight off an iPhone, or a PDF or TIFF that came from a floor-plan vendorConvert to JPEG or PNG before delivery
File too largeAn unresized raw conversion, often a single 40 MB frame in an otherwise fine setRe-export at a sensible quality; the floor here is 20 MB per file
Odd cropA panorama, a hand-trimmed shot, or a screenshot of a photoRecrop to a standard listing shape: 4:3, 3:2, 16:9, 5:4 or square
BrandingA logo, watermark, headshot or brokerage card that got copied into the folderRemove it from the set. Listing images show the property, not the agent
Undisclosed stagingA virtually staged room delivered without its unaltered counterpartLabel it and deliver the unstaged version of the same room alongside it

Why these particular things

The listing does not stop at the MLS. The same images syndicate out to portals, each of which resizes and re-crops them into its own frame. A file that is just large enough for the board is often not large enough after that, and an unusual crop gets cut again by something with no opinion about which half of the kitchen matters.

Branding on a photo is a policy question, not a taste one. Boards differ, but the common position is that listing images carry the property and nothing else, because the display surface belongs to whoever is showing it. A logo in the corner is the sort of thing that gets a whole set kicked back rather than one file.

Staging disclosure is where the real exposure sits. A too-small photo costs an hour. A digitally altered room presented as the room can be a misrepresentation problem, which is why disclosure requirements are widespread and why a staged file delivered on its own is worth flagging even when nobody has rejected it yet.

What a preflight can and cannot tell you

The checker on this site reads file headers, pixel dimensions and filenames. From those it can decide resolution, format, byte size, crop shape, branding tokens in a name, and whether a staged photo is paired. It produces a dated record of what it checked, which is useful to keep with the delivery.

It cannot see a watermark burned into the pixels, contact details printed inside the image, or anything your board requires that is not visible in a file header — and it names those exclusions in its own output rather than leaving you to assume they were covered. It is a floor, not your board's rulebook. The rules that apply to you are the ones in your board's current photo standards; this catches the mechanical failures early so that the only thing left to review is the photography.

Check the folder before you send it

Drop in the delivery folder and see every file that would bounce, and why, in one pass. It runs entirely in your browser — the photos are never uploaded, and there is no account.

Open the free listing photo preflight

Common questions

Why was my listing photo rejected?

Most rejections come from something readable in the file rather than from the picture itself: the image is too small on its long edge, the file is in a format the system does not take, it is too large to upload, the crop is not a standard listing shape, or the filename or the image carries brokerage branding, a watermark or a headshot. Virtual staging that is not disclosed is the other common one. Every item on that list can be checked before delivery, which is what the free preflight on this site does.

What is the minimum size for an MLS listing photo?

Boards set their own numbers, so the only correct answer for you is the one in your own board's current photo standards. The floor this tool checks is 1024 pixels on the long edge, which is deliberately conservative: an image under it is too small for essentially any board and for the syndication portals a listing feeds into. Clearing that floor is not the same as meeting your board's requirement, which may well be higher.

Can I put my logo or my brokerage name on a listing photo?

Usually not on the photos themselves. Rules vary by board, but the common position is that listing images show the property and not the agent, because the same images syndicate out to portals that display their own branding. This checker flags a filename containing logo, watermark, branded, brokerage or headshot as a warning, since those names are the usual sign that a branded asset has been dropped into a delivery folder by mistake. It reads names and headers only, so it cannot see a watermark burned into the pixels.

Do I have to label a virtually staged photo?

Assume yes and check your board's wording. Disclosure of digitally altered or virtually staged images is a widespread requirement, and the usual practice is both a label on the image and an unaltered version of the same room available alongside it. This tool looks for staged, virtually-staged or virtual-staged in filenames and checks that a staged photo is paired rather than delivered on its own; it cannot tell you what your board's disclosure text has to say.

Why does a photo get flagged for its aspect ratio?

Because an unusual crop is nearly always accidental, and a listing system that fits every image into one frame will crop it again to fit. The checker accepts the standard listing shapes in either orientation, 4:3, 3:2, 16:9, 5:4 and square, within a small tolerance. Something outside those is typically a screenshot, a phone panorama, or a photo trimmed by hand, and it is worth looking at before it becomes the shot the portal decides to cut in half.

Does this replace my MLS board's photo rules?

No, and it is not trying to. It is a dated floor spec covering what can be decided from a file header and a filename, so it catches the mechanical rejections early and says plainly what it cannot see: a watermark burned into the image, contact details inside the picture, and every board-specific rule. Read it as a preflight that saves you a round trip, not as a compliance sign-off.
